question:
Patient note:
A 61-year-old man is reviewed in the ambulatory procedure bay while nursing staff complete a timeout for a planned arthroscopic debridement and rotator-cuff anchor repair of the dominant right shoulder, an operation the orthopedic team estimates will occupy the glenohumeral joint for roughly ninety minutes under general anesthesia with an interscalene nerve block and same-day discharge if he meets recovery criteria. He arrived on foot from the parking deck, negotiated two flights of stairs without pausing, and matter-of-factly reports that he still bicycles four miles along a canal towpath most mornings despite chronic shortness of breath from long-standing tobacco-related lung disease; he keeps a rescue inhaler in his jersey pocket but has not required systemic steroids or emergency visits this season. Pulmonary clinic letters in the electronic chart document moderate airflow obstruction on spirometry, a baseline oxygen saturation of 94 % on room air, and no need for supplemental oxygen outside acute exacerbations. He has not been hospitalized for pneumonia, bacteremia, or any infection meeting sepsis criteria within the past thirty days. Sixteen days ago, during evaluation of purulent sputum and wheeze that never progressed to systemic hypotension or organ dysfunction, hospitalists placed a single-lumen peripherally inserted central catheter in the right basilic vein for a planned fourteen-day course of intravenous levofloxacin; that catheter remains tunneled to the mid-upper arm today beneath an intact occlusive dressing, flushes freely with saline, and shows no erythema, induration, or tenderness along its course. He has otherwise avoided operating rooms, endoscopy suites, or interventional radiology in the past year and confirms that he has not undergone any procedure requiring general, regional, or monitored anesthesia care in the last thirty days. He denies recent fractures of the hip, pelvis, or lower extremities, has not worn any immobilizing casts or braces, and has had no spinal cord injuries, strokes, or transient neurologic attacks over the same period. Review of recent events is negative for fever, rigors, pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, calf cramping, unilateral leg swelling, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, transient neurological deficits, abdominal pain, traumatic injury, or prolonged immobilization. Past medical history is notable for diet-controlled type 2 diabetes, hypertension managed with lisinopril, and a heterozygous mutation in the prothrombin G20210A gene identified five years ago after his younger sister developed an unprovoked iliofemoral clot while on a transpacific flight; although he himself has never experienced venous or arterial thrombosis, he recalls that both his mother and an aunt required blood thinners during pregnancy-related clotting events. He specifically denies physician-diagnosed lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibodies, platelet factor-4 antibodies, or other named coagulation disorders, and states he has never had heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. There is no history of inflammatory bowel disease, malignant tumors, myocardial infarction, or heart-failure admissions. He quit a 40-pack-year smoking habit eight years ago, enjoys a single whiskey on Friday evenings, and does not use recreational drugs. Current medications include tiotropium once daily, albuterol as needed, lisinopril 20 mg, and over-the-counter fish-oil capsules; no glucocorticoids, hormone therapy, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, selective estrogen-receptor modulators, or antiplatelet drugs are taken. Vital signs obtained ten minutes ago reveal temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 132/78 mm Hg, pulse 72 beats min⁻¹ in regular rhythm, respiratory rate 14 min⁻¹, and oxygen saturation 95 % breathing ambient air; body-mass index is 26 kg m⁻². He is alert, oriented, and converses easily without accessory-muscle use. Airway assessment shows Mallampati class II, more than three finger-breadth mouth opening, thyromental distance six centimeters, and good cervical extension. Cardiovascular examination displays a nondisplaced apical impulse and crisp S₁/S₂ without murmurs, rubs, or gallops; jugular venous contour is below the sternal angle at 30°. Lung fields reveal bilateral scattered end-expiratory wheezes that clear with coughing, no crackles, and symmetric excursion. Abdomen is soft, non-tender, and without organomegaly or surgical scars. Inspection of both lower extremities shows normal color, temperature, and hair distribution; there are no tortuous superficial veins, pitting edema, calf tenderness, or side-to-side circumference difference measured ten centimeters below the tibial tuberosity (both 35 cm). Posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis pulses are 2+/4 bilaterally. Neurologic screening demonstrates 5/5 strength in all muscle groups, intact sensation to light touch, and a smooth tandem gait witnessed when he walked unassisted to the restroom moments ago. The right shoulder exhibits visible supraspinatus wasting and painful arc above 90°, while the contralateral joint has full painless motion. A 20-gauge peripheral IV in the left antecubital fossa runs lactated Ringer’s at keep-open rate in addition to the dormant PICC line. Morning laboratory values drawn through the catheter at 05:45 show hemoglobin 14.0 g dL⁻¹, hematocrit 42 %, platelets 248 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, leukocytes 7.2 × 10⁹ L⁻¹, sodium 137 mmol L⁻¹, potassium 4.0 mmol L⁻¹, bicarbonate 24 mmol L⁻¹, creatinine 0.90 mg dL⁻¹, AST 20 U L⁻¹, ALT 22 U L⁻¹, total bilirubin 0.7 mg dL⁻¹, prothrombin time 12.3 s with an international normalized ratio of 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 29 s. A twelve-lead electrocardiogram acquired on arrival shows normal sinus rhythm at 70 beats min⁻¹ with nonspecific ST-T changes identical to previous tracings. Postero-anterior and lateral chest radiographs from yesterday demonstrate hyperinflated lung fields without focal infiltrate or mass and confirm the PICC tip at the cavo-atrial junction. Sequential intermittent pneumatic compression devices are at the foot of the stretcher awaiting activation after induction; pharmacologic prophylaxis has been deferred until surgical hemostasis is confirmed. He has been nil per os since midnight, last voided at 0600, removed his dental bridge, and demonstrates clear understanding of the operative plan, post-anesthesia expectations, and the importance of continuing range-of-motion exercises once the sling is discontinued.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini surgical VTE risk score sums the applicable preoperative risk factors:
- Age 61 (61–74 years) → 2.
- BMI 26 kg/m² (>25) → 1.
- COPD with abnormal pulmonary function → 1.
- Planned 90-minute arthroscopic surgery → 2. Count the operation once, not separately for arthroscopy and duration >45 minutes.
- Central venous access: indwelling PICC → 2. The peripheral IV adds nothing.
- Family history of VTE: sister with an iliofemoral clot → 3, counted once regardless of the number of affected relatives.
- Inherited thrombophilia: prothrombin G20210A mutation → 3, distinct from family history.
No personal VTE, recent major surgery, qualifying immobility, or other documented scoring factor adds points. Total: 2 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 3 = 14.
Final answer: 14
